competitors.description:
Anchorage Digital Adds TRON Support Within a Federally Chartered Custody Framework

The integration of the TRON network into the custody services of Anchorage Digital reflects the extension of blockchain asset support into a regulated financial environment. Anchorage Digital operates as a federally chartered crypto bank in the United States, providing custody and infrastructure services for digital assets under established regulatory oversight.

This development places TRON assets within a custody framework that adheres to compliance standards associated with federally chartered institutions. Such institutions operate under defined regulatory supervision, with requirements covering asset safeguarding, operational controls, risk management, and reporting procedures. The inclusion of TRON within this environment allows institutional participants to access and hold TRON-based assets through a platform designed for regulated financial operations.

Custody solutions offered by federally chartered entities typically focus on secure storage of private keys, segregation of client assets, and protection against unauthorized access. These systems are designed to support institutional usage, where asset security, auditability, and operational reliability are essential components of service delivery.

The expansion of support for TRON within this context also aligns with broader trends in digital asset infrastructure, where blockchain networks are integrated into platforms that serve institutional clients. This integration supports standardized access to assets while maintaining alignment with compliance requirements applicable to regulated financial services providers.

The presence of TRON within Anchorage Digital’s custody framework establishes a channel through which institutional participants can interact with the network using infrastructure that operates under formal regulatory supervision, contributing to structured adoption within the digital asset ecosystem.

That gap is now being addressed.
